idiom_name: temp-val/var rebinding (no stdlib swap; Collections.swap and AtomicReference by JVM interop)
implementation_notes: Scala's collection library has no swap - mutable sequences such as ArrayBuffer expose only update/insert/remove - so the exchange is written locally: `val t = a; a = b; b = t`, or, for a class, one var holding the whole state whose rebinding is a plain reference assignment that cannot allocate or throw. That replaces the classic C++ structure completely (no noexcept, no ADL, no customization point); where a list exchange is wanted, java.util.Collections.swap(list, i, j) is available through the JVM interop, and for state shared between threads java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference (or a @volatile var for visibility only). Two atomic references cannot be exchanged as a pair, so everything that must change together stays behind one immutable holder.
pitfalls: Function parameters are vals, so a swap must write to vars or a mutable holder; `val (a, b) = (b, a)` creates new bindings rather than exchanging existing ones.

Two separate assignments are not atomic (@volatile gives visibility but no exchange primitive), so readers can observe the intermediate state where both references point at the same value; publish one immutable reference instead.
Collections.swap and ArrayBuffer.update throw IndexOutOfBoundsException, so a rollback path cannot call them as if they were infallible.
A var that implements an abstract var from a trait can end up with two backing fields when trait and class initialization order differ - the "single state handle" then is not single after all.
